title: What is normal sleep?
intro: Sleep is a vital, active state in which the body repairs itself and the brain processes memories. How much sleep people need varies, and so does the timing. Knowing what is normal can help you recognise sleep problems and build healthy sleep habits.

sections.heading: How much sleep is needed
paragraphs: Most adults need seven to nine hours a night. Teenagers need eight to ten hours, school-age children nine to twelve, and babies much more. Older people often sleep less deeply and wake more easily but still need about seven to eight hours. Some people feel fine with a little less or more.

sections.heading: Stages of sleep
paragraphs: Sleep goes through cycles of about ninety minutes. Light sleep leads into deep sleep, which is important for physical recovery, and rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, when most dreams occur and the brain processes emotion and memory. Several cycles happen each night, with more deep sleep early and more REM sleep later.

sections.heading: Body clock
paragraphs: An internal clock, the circadian rhythm, regulates sleep and wakefulness over about twenty-four hours, responding to light and darkness. Teenagers shift later, while older adults tend to wake earlier. Shift work, travel and bright screens at night can disturb the rhythm. Morning daylight helps keep it steady.

sections.heading: Normal variations
paragraphs: Taking up to half an hour to fall asleep, waking briefly during the night, dreaming and mild snoring can be normal. Occasional poor nights are common and usually not harmful. Persistent difficulty falling or staying asleep, loud snoring with breathing pauses, daytime sleepiness or restless legs may signal a sleep disorder.

sections.heading: Healthy sleep habits
paragraphs: Keep regular times for sleeping and waking, make the bedroom dark, quiet and cool, avoid caffeine late in the day, limit alcohol and heavy meals near bedtime, stay active in daytime and reduce screen use before bed. If you cannot sleep, get up and do something relaxing, then return when sleepy.

examples.title: Setting a routine
examples.text: Imagine you often sleep badly. You could go to bed and rise at the same times every day and limit screens an hour beforehand.

examples.title: Seeking advice
examples.text: Suppose you snore loudly and feel exhausted by day. You might ask your doctor about a test for sleep apnoea.
